title: So 'ham: the one behind the sun
hookLine: a voice asks the sun to draw back its golden light, sees who stands behind it, and the answer is in every breath
carry: so 'ham: the breath says that one, i am
tomorrow: what did an old teacher tell students who were leaving home?

lines: A VOICE TURNS TO THE SUN.
cards: Near the end of the Isha Upanishad, one of the shortest and most loved, a voice turns to the sun and asks for one thing. The face of truth, it says, is hidden behind a golden disc.
Draw it back, so that I, who keep to truth, may see. Spread out your rays. Gather in your blinding light.
Many readers hear these as words spoken near the end of a life. And then the voice sees, and says what it sees: that person there, in the light. So 'ham asmi.

teach.b: That one, I am. Many teachers hear it as the same discovery Shvetaketu's father pointed to with salt in water: the light you looked for out there and the self in here are not strangers.
Look how the words are built, because the join tells the story too.
Sah, that one, and aham, I. The -ah of sah turns to o, and the o swallows the short a of aham. What's left is so 'ham.
In Devanagari, a small curl called the avagraha stands where the a went. It makes no sound. Two words, one breath.
And Hindu tradition took that breath literally. In some yoga traditions, so is heard riding the breath in and ham riding it out, a mantra the body repeats all day without being asked.
They call it ajapa japa: the repetition nobody recites. Japa, repeating a sacred name or mantra, is one of the most common Hindu practices, often counted on a mala of a hundred and eight beads.
Ajapa japa is japa that's already going on. Turn the words around and they become hamsa, the swan, an old image for the soul.

teach.h: AS NEAR AS YOUR NEXT BREATH.
teach.b: So the teaching is this: the Self that a seer looked for behind the sun is as near as your next breath, and a Hindu can turn toward it without saying a word.

how: Many Hindus do japa, repeating a mantra or a name of God, often on a mala of 108 beads; some yoga traditions pair so with the in-breath and ham with the out-breath as a quiet, unspoken japa. Printed Sanskrit marks the dropped a with the avagraha (ऽ).

o: a breathing rule for chanting long lines
the sign that tells a singer to pause
undoing joins, even ones that leave a silent mark

games.q: so 'ham, taken apart — tap the pairs.
p: said of the person in the sun's light
the mantra the breath repeats unasked
the silent curl for a dropped a

s: so 'ham is a modern wellness phrase
the Isha Upanishad has so 'ham asmi: the person in the light, that one I am.
japa means repeating a sacred name or mantra, often on a mala
ajapa japa is the same repetition, heard in the breath.
in the Isha, the voice asks the sun for more light to see by
it asks the sun to gather in its blinding light, so the truth behind it can be seen.

games.q: your aunt quietly repeats so 'ham on her mala before bed. your little cousin asks what it means. what do you say?
o: 'that one, I am': the light the old seer saw behind the sun is in you too, as near as your breath.
it's a sleepy sound, like counting sheep; it doesn't mean anything.
it's a spell to keep bad dreams away.
games.why: so 'ham is sah plus aham, that one, I. in the Isha it's what the seer says on seeing the person in the light; in japa, it rides the breath.

practice: Let the breath become just a little audible, and listen to it. On the way in there may be a soft s, on the way out something closer to a hum.
If you pray, think so as the breath comes in and ham as it goes out, the way people do with japa. If you don't, simply listen. Notice the small gap where the breath turns.
If a thought comes, let it leave on the out-breath, and come back to the sound.

wordCard.voice: Sandhi plainly: words meeting and changing. Today, sah and aham becoming so 'ham, and a silent curl keeping the place of the a.

orig.note: Sanskrit: so 'ham, that one I am; the ऽ is the avagraha.

carryVoice: Pocket this: so 'ham, the breath says that one, I am. The seer looked behind the sun; it was this close. Rest well.

sources.ref: Isha Upanishad 15–16 (the golden disc over the face of truth; so 'ham asmi)
Ashtadhyayi 6.1.109 (enah padantad ati: a short a after word-final e or o is dropped)
so 'ham / hamsa as the breath's unrecited mantra (ajapa japa)
